summary: Provides the framework for dynamic provisioning of MPLS-TP transport paths using a control plane, covering addressing, routing, path computation, signaling, traffic engineering, and recovery. MPLS-TP uses GMPLS as its control plane. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Paths can be set up by hand or by automatic software. This explains how the automatic version works for MPLS-TP networks, using the GMPLS tool set.

questions: how do you set up mpls-tp paths dynamically
subtitle: Framework for automatic provisioning of MPLS Transport Profile paths

tldr.problem: Operators deploying MPLS-TP as a transport technology need a way to dynamically set up paths without manual configuration, similar to other transport networks.
tldr.mechanism: The framework uses GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) with RSVP-TE for label-switched paths and LDP for pseudowires, combined with OSPF or ISIS routing.
tldr.outcome: MPLS-TP can be deployed with automatic path setup, recovery, and management, bridging a gap between traditional packet networks and telecommunications infrastructure.

facts.label: LSP types
facts.value: Unidirectional, bidirectional co-routed, bidirectional associated, point-to-point, point-to-multipoint

today: RFC 6373 is Informational and remains a foundational document for MPLS-TP control plane deployments. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the current framework for understanding how MPLS-TP paths are dynamically provisioned.

sections.title: Introducing MPLS-TP and its Control Plane
sections.content:
The Multiprotocol Label Switching Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is a joint effort between the IETF and ITU-T to create a transport network that uses MPLS data-plane technology but operates like telecommunications equipment. It can carry voice, video, and data as connection-oriented services with guaranteed capacity and protection.

MPLS-TP allows two ways to set up paths: static provisioning (an operator types in the configuration for each path by hand via a management system) and dynamic provisioning (the network automatically calculates and sets up paths on demand). This document defines the framework for the dynamic control plane, addressing routing, path computation, signaling, traffic engineering, and recovery mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone networks need to automatically set up the routes that data travels on, just like the internet does, but with guarantees that the data gets there and arrives in order. This RFC explains how to do that.

sections.title: Control Plane Architecture and Reference Points
sections.content:
The MPLS-TP control plane is based on Generalized MPLS (GMPLS), which extends MPLS to support not just packet-switched networks but also optical and time-division-multiplexed networks. The framework defines three types of reference points: UNI (User-to-Network Interface) where customers connect to the operator's network, I-NNI (Internal Network-to-Network Interface) within a single operator's network, and E-NNI (External NNI) between different operators' networks.

The control plane can operate in-band (using the same channel as data traffic) or out-of-band (using a separate management channel). The framework supports the separation of control, management, and data planes so they can use different addresses and even different network topologies, which is essential for resilient transport networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The control plane is the 'brain' that decides where data goes. It can talk to customers at the edge, between operators' networks, and internally. It can send its instructions through the data channel or use a separate phone line, and doesn't have to follow the same routes as the actual data.

sections.title: Label Switched Path Control via GMPLS RSVP-TE
sections.content:
Label Switched Paths (LSPs) are the end-to-end tunnels that carry traffic across an MPLS-TP network. The framework specifies that GMPLS RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol with Traffic Engineering extensions) handles LSP signaling and path setup. RSVP-TE uses routing information from OSPF-TE or ISIS-TE to compute constraint-based paths that respect bandwidth reservations, link costs, and other constraints.

GMPLS supports both point-to-point LSPs (one source to one destination) and point-to-multipoint LSPs (one source to multiple destinations). It also allows bidirectional LSPs where traffic can flow in both directions, with a choice between co-routed (following the same path in both directions) and associated bidirectional paths (where forward and backward paths may differ). The framework also defines support for hierarchical LSPs, where one LSP can nest inside another for scaling and recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network needs to send data from point A to point B, the control plane uses a protocol (RSVP-TE) that asks 'is there a path with 100 Mbps free?' and then books the route. It can handle sending data in both directions, splitting across multiple destinations, or nesting tunnels inside each other like Russian dolls.

sections.title: Pseudowire Signaling and Multi-Segment Support
sections.content:
Pseudowires (PWs) emulate layer 2 services such as Ethernet or ATM across an MPLS network. Unlike LSPs, which are controlled by GMPLS RSVP-TE, pseudowires use the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), specifically targeted LDP, for signaling. This allows the PW control plane to operate independently of LSP control. A single-segment pseudowire connects two provider edge nodes directly, while a multi-segment pseudowire is stitched together from multiple segments, each controlled separately.

The framework specifies that PWs can carry native layer 2 services end-to-end, and that PW segments can be aggregated inside LSP tunnels. This combination allows flexible network design: for example, many edge nodes can have simple static PW configuration, while a central node coordinates the PSN tunnels. The independence of PW and LSP control planes means operators can choose which to deploy; they can use both, just LSPs, just PWs, or neither (static provisioning).
sections.plainLanguage: Pseudowires are like virtual cables that copy layer 2 services (like Ethernet) across the network. They use a different control protocol (LDP) than LSPs, so they can be set up independently. You can also chain them together in segments and hide them inside LSP tunnels.

sections.title: Protection, Recovery, and OAM Signaling
sections.content:
Transport networks must recover from failures quickly—often in under 50 milliseconds. The framework incorporates GMPLS recovery mechanisms including 1+1 protection (two paths, always using the working path until it fails), 1:n protection (one working path and n backup paths, one of which takes over on failure), and mesh restoration (using spare capacity across the network to reroute traffic). Shared mesh restoration is particularly valuable because many backup paths can reuse the same network resources, reducing cost.

The control plane must also support Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM). OAM functions include continuity checks (is the path alive?), connectivity verification (am I connected to the right peer?), performance measurement, and fault detection. The framework requires that the control plane configure OAM entities (Maintenance Entity Points and Intermediate Points) when paths are set up, so monitoring can be activated automatically without manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: When a cable breaks, the network must automatically reroute traffic in milliseconds. The control plane sets up backup paths ahead of time, and when a failure happens, switches over instantly. It also automatically turns on health checks so you know if something is wrong.

sections.title: Integration with MPLS and Interoperability
sections.content:
The framework reflects 141 detailed requirements derived from other MPLS-TP documents. Key principles include reusing existing IETF MPLS and GMPLS standards wherever possible, ensuring interoperability between vendors, and supporting coexistence of static and dynamic provisioning in the same network. The control plane must scale to large networks (hundreds or thousands of nodes and paths) and work across multiple domains operated by different providers.

The framework also emphasizes that control-plane operation must be independent of the management and data planes, allowing each to have its own topology and addressing scheme. Finally, the control plane must be able to restart and recover its previous state (graceful restart) without disrupting the data paths it has already set up, ensuring that a control-plane failure does not cause packet loss for traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TP reuses the tools MPLS already has instead of inventing new ones. It works across multiple operators' networks and different vendors' equipment. And if the control plane crashes, the data keeps flowing without interruption.
